question: The European Union is at a critical juncture in its enlargement strategy. Recent reports suggest plans to accelerate the accession process of Ukraine, Türkiye or other Balkan countries, even bypassing the unanimity principle, in order to overcome possible vetoes by Member States.

1 At the same time, in its public interventions the Commission stresses the need for ‘renewed momentum’ for the enlargement process,2 while public opinion in Europe — as recorded in the recent Eurobarometer3 — calls for protection, unity and stability as a priority.

Rapidly advancing enlargement without a parallel strengthening of institutions and without clear measures to maintain social cohesion could create serious problems: destabilizing the EU, undermining its democratic functioning and eroding citizens' trust. In view of the above: 1.
How does the Commission intend to ensure that enlargement does not undermine the cohesion, functionality and legitimacy of the EU?
Does the Commission intend to make a commitment that no decision on the decisionmaking process, such as the abolition of unanimity, will be taken without the full unanimity of the Member States?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.10.2025) The enlargement process is and remains a strict, fair and merit-based process, based on the objective progress achieved by each enlargement country, in line with the Copenhagen criteria.
This process aims to ensure that the EU will continue to deliver and function as was the case in previous enlargements, and not undermine the cohesion, functionality and legitimacy of the EU.

Moreover, following the Communication of March 2024 on pre-enlargement reforms and policy reviews1, the Commission is currently carrying out pre-enlargement reviews, assessing the extent to which policies and governance of the EU will be affected by future enlargement and what changes could be considered to address any identified gaps.
The Commission recalls that under the EU Treaties, any decision to move from unanimity to qualified majority voting in Council requires the unanimous support by all Member States.
